blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a large-scale qualitative study from ICSE'18 that examines 'licensing bugs'—issues developers face when dealing with software licenses. The paper presents a comprehensive catalog of seven major categories and 21 sub-categories of licensing bugs, derived from analyzing 1,200 discussions across issue trackers and mailing lists. Colyer notes the study's practical value, especially for developers and lawyers, despite the authors not being legal experts. The taxonomy covers a wide range of licensing challenges, from legal interpretations (e.g., derivative works, copyright scope) to ecosystem policies (e.g., community guidelines) and non-source code artifacts (e.g., fonts, images). The paper also explores license incompatibilities, content licensing inconsistencies, and intellectual property rights issues like CLAs and CTAs. Colyer emphasizes the study's relevance to stakeholders such as integrators, distributors, and package maintainers, and its potential to inform better licensing practices in open-source communities.
paper_title: To distribute or not to distribute? Why licensing bugs matter
paper_abstract: 1 Software licenses dictate how source code or binaries can be modified, reused, and redistributed. In the case of open source projects, software licenses generally fit into two main categories, permissive and restrictive, depending on the degree to which they allow redistribution or modification under licenses different from the original one(s). Developers and organizations can also modify existing licenses, creating custom licenses with specific permissive/restrictive terms. Having such a variety of software licenses can create confusion among software developers, and can easily result in the introduction of licensing bugs, not necessarily limited to well-known license incompatibilities. In this work, we report a study aimed at characterizing licensing bugs by (i) building a catalog categorizing the types of licensing bugs developers and other stakeholders face, and (ii) understanding the implications licensing bugs have on the software projects they affect. The presented study is the result of the manual analysis of 1,200 discussions related to licensing bugs carried out in issue trackers and in five legal mailing lists of open source communities. Our findings uncover new types of licensing bugs not addressed in prior literature, and a detailed assessment of their implications. Software licenses define the terms under which a software system (either its code or binary) can legally be distributed, modified, and reused. As of today, there are over 100 known open source software licenses [61, 62]. In a broad sense, licenses can be divided into two categories: restrictive licenses (such as the General Public License—GPL—family of licenses), requiring the redistribution of derivative work under the same licensing terms, and permissive licenses, which impose few restrictions (such as the MIT license).
